name: PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Tambangraya Megah: a net-cash, high-CV Kalimantan producer priced as if the cycle is over
frontmatter.summary: ITM sells high-CV Kalimantan coal at a stable discount to the Newcastle marker, runs with net cash and pays a variable dividend. Our through-cycle NAV sits below the tape, but the dividend cross-check and the near-term tonne economics put the total return positive; we initiate at ADD, the base case below spot and the bull case carried by the war premium.
thesis: Realisation is a level, not a trend: our fitted export realisation reproduces the FY2025 actual blended price and the FY2024 year checks to within a few percent on the same basis, so the base case is not fitted to the war-premium spike.

Volume is the company's own plan, not our call: FY2026E sits inside the published indicative sales range and is held flat afterwards, because the stated reserve base supports roughly a decade and a half at that rate and nothing in the mine plan sources a fade.

The balance sheet is the hinge: net cash, a small debt line and a standing buyback authorisation mean the dividend and the capital return, not the life-of-asset NAV, are what the market is capitalising.
Costs hold the last actual in real terms and then follow the mine plan's stripping sequence, sourced to the company's own quarterly strip-ratio guidance rather than to a cautious default.

The bear is the mirror of the bull on the same four drivers: the benchmark moved by the same proportion in each direction, volume clipped by half the sizing of the disclosed quota risk, and royalty and the required return moved in opposite directions.

catalysts.event: Third-quarter FY2026 production and sales release; check sales against the indicative range and the strip-ratio sequence
FY2027 RKAB approval from ESDM; the quota sets next year's volume line
Annual general meeting: final dividend declaration and progress on the standing buyback authorisation
Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I) concession expiry; watch the extension or conversion route

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk at **ADD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp26,442** against a last price of Rp25,500, a total return of **19.1%** on our probability-weighted scenarios and a price-only upside of 3.7% before the dividend stream. The company is the Indonesian thermal-coal arm of the Banpu group: four CCoW concessions in East and Central Kalimantan plus a clutch of IUPs, producing a high-calorific-value product, with the Imm and Tcm coals well up the grade range [S2], sold to China, Japan, India and the domestic power market from a net-cash balance sheet [S3].

Our through-cycle life-of-asset NAV is **Rp17,712**, below the tape, because the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker mean-reverts well below the spot print and we value the reserve life, not the war premium [S0]. What lifts the target above that NAV is the dividend: on the modelled payout the shares support a dividend-capacity yield that capitalises at **Rp34,806** [S0], and the market has historically paid ITMG on that anchor rather than on the reserve value. The two cross-checks bracket the primary method on opposite sides — EV/EBITDA at Rp34,101 (92.5% above the DCF) and the dividend method at Rp34,806 (96.5% above) — which is the honest picture of a name whose equity value sits between its reserve value and its cash-return capacity.

The variant view, stated plainly: the market is capitalising a low-yield dividend at close to the cash return it can actually sustain, and it is doing so at a price that implies the Newcastle benchmark holds near **US$130/t** through the horizon, a factor of 1.1 on the deck's own first forecast-year marker [S0]. We think that is too generous on price and too harsh on volume: our volume path is the company's own plan, our realisation is calibrated on two consecutive actual years, and our costs hold the last actual in real terms and then follow the mine plan's stripping sequence [S3, S2]. Three things move the value: the Newcastle benchmark through the horizon, the RKAB quota that sets the volume line, and the share of tonnes the government diverts to the domestic power market under the standing cap [S2, S3].

PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal producer, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007 and now a subsidiary of Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., which holds 66.3% of the shares with the balance in public hands [S2]. It reports in US dollars, sells in US dollars, and employs 1,609.0 people [S0]. The group's own structure slide shows the controlling chain — Banpu at roughly two thirds, the public at roughly a third, and a small treasury-share position [S2].

The business is a single commodity with a diversified mine portfolio. Production comes from four CCoW concessions — Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I, East Kalimantan), Trubaindo Coal Mining (CCOW Gen II, East Kalimantan), Bharinto Ekatama (CCOW Gen III, East and Central Kalimantan) and Jorong Barutama Greston (CCOW Gen II, South Kalimantan) — together with four IUPs: Graha Panca Karsa, Tepian Indah Sukses, Nusa Persada Resources and Kitadin [S3]. The product mix is skewed to the higher grades: the Imm, Tcm and Bek coals are the high-calorific-value grades while Jbg, Gpk and Npr sit lower down the range [S2]. That grade mix is the single most important fact about the name: it is what makes the realised price key off the Newcastle and HBA markers rather than the low-grade ICI indices [S2].

Alongside the coal book the group runs adjacent businesses that are small against it but strategically named: coal trading through an energy-commodities subsidiary, mining contractor and port services, and a renewable-energy arm building rooftop solar [S2]. In October 2026 the group stood up a further subsidiary in the mineral sector to hold a diversification portfolio [S4]. None of these is material to value at this stage. The solar book is delivered to customers as a service rather than owned outright, the Bunyut port works are capitalised inside the coal cost base, and the new mineral vehicle is funded from internal cash with no separately disclosed carrying value, so we carry the diversification at nil in the bridge and say why rather than inventing a project value [S3, S4].

The competitive position is that of a mid-sized, high-grade, low-cost Indonesian producer: large enough on the seaborne trade to be a price-taker on the marker but with a grade and a cost position that keep it in the first part of the global cost curve [S3]. Its reserve base at the end of 2025 was 382 Mt of JORC reserves against a resource inventory several times larger, with the nearest expiry the Indominco Mandiri CCoW Gen I concession in March 2028 and the IUP mines running out into the following decade [S2]. The Indominco concession is the nearest expiry and the nearest policy question, and we flag it in the risk section.

Thermal coal is a cyclical, dollar-priced, policy-shaped commodity, and the deck we work from frames it that way: the Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg marker is the price series, the DMO cap is the administered ceiling on domestic power tonnes, and the coal deck's long-run view is that the marginal Indonesian tonne clears in a band around its long-run marker once the war premium fades [S0]. Our industry read is that supply discipline, not demand growth, is what has held the price up: the company's own market commentary names Indonesian RKAB uncertainty and higher domestic-market obligations as the supply constraint, alongside logistics disruption in South Africa and Colombia and the war-driven diesel shortage in Russia, with Chinese domestic output and Indian import substitution the two demand-side dampeners [S2].

Regulation is the swing factor and it is specific. Indonesian coal sits under the RKAB annual work-plan-and-budget approval, which sets each producer's permitted volume, and under the domestic market obligation that reserves a share of output for the national power market at the administered cap [S2, S3]. The royalty regime depends on the licence: the group's CCoW mines pay a contract-specific rate while the IUP mines pay the lower IUP schedule, and the royalty expense the group actually books, on the LK's own numbers, was 220 USD m of royalty expense on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in the last financial year, an effective rate well below the contract headline [S3]. We set the licence parameter to the work-agreement (contract) regime the group actually books under rather than the newer IUPK schedule, and the royalty to the effective booked rate, and explain why in the valuation section and in the model's own justification.

The competitive landscape is the Indonesian seaborne cohort — the other listed producers on this desk — and the moat is grade and cost position rather than scale: a high-CV product with a first-quartile cash cost is what survives a trough, and ITM's strip ratio and unit cost sit in that part of the curve [S3]. Its pricing power is nil on the marker and real on the mix: because the product sits at the top of the grade range, a given move in the Newcastle marker passes through to ITM's realised price at a stable ratio, which is the property we rely on when we calibrate the realisation either side of the last two actual years [S3, S5]. On the five forces, supplier power is moderate (contract mining and fuel, with diesel the live cost pressure the company itself names), buyer power is high (a commodity market with many sellers), the threat of substitutes is real but slow — and the near-term switching runs the other way, as the company's own market note observes, with gas-to-coal switching in Japan, Korea and Taiwan holding thermal demand firm [S2] — new-entrant risk is low (permits, capital and the RKAB gate), and rivalry is high but disciplined by the same permit regime that limits output. The external influences that matter for the numbers are the Newcastle marker, the rupiah, and the domestic-market share the government takes.

The five-year record is a classic coal cycle. Revenue ran at US$3,636.2m in the peak year, fell to US$2,374.3m and US$2,304.5m, and reached US$1,881.1m in the last actual year [S0, S3]. The compression is entirely price: volumes were steady at 24.0 and 24.7 of sales tonnage in the last two years [S3], while the realised price fell from 95.7 to 76.0 [S5]. Gross margin narrowed with it, and net profit to parent fell to US$190.9m [S0].

Our forecast rebuilds the same way. Revenue is volume times a capped realised price: volume is the company's own FY2026 indicative range, held flat afterwards, and the price is the deck's Newcastle marker times a realisation ratio we calibrated on the last two actual years and hold constant [S3, S2, S0]. That gives first-forecast-year revenue of US$2,502.0m at a realised price of 92.0, against 76.0 in the last actual year, and an EBITDA of US$561.7m [S0].

Costs are the part of the model where caution usually creeps in, and we have kept it out. The cash cost per tonne is built from the physical stripping ratio and the mining cost per cubic metre plus a residual for hauling, barging, processing and the purchased-coal book, and the mining cost per cubic metre is itself backed out of the LK's own cost-of-revenue note rather than asserted [S3]. The stripping ratio is set to the current run-rate rather than the last full year's average, because the company's own quarterly disclosure has the pits deepening, the ratio already above the FY2025A level and guided higher again [S2] — the group's own presentation shows the ratio rising through the first half as the pits deepen [S2]. Royalty is the effective rate the LK books, not the contract headline [S3], and SG&A is carried at the last actual's share of revenue because the step-up in selling and administrative cost in the last year reads as structural rather than cyclical [S3].

We restate the depreciation line rather than modelling around it. The data pack's most recent figure is in the right region but its prior-year figure is a stub, because the Indonesian cash-flow statement uses the direct method and carries no D&A add-back; we take the LK's own depreciation charge from the cost-of-revenue note for the last two fiscal years and let the engine rebuild history from them [S3]. Capex is split between sustaining spend per tonne, held flat in nominal terms so it declines in real terms, and expansion spend for the port capacity works, the solar pipeline and the new mineral vehicle, stepped down as those programmes complete [S3, S2, S4]. Working capital is thin and held at the historical ratio; the balance sheet is net cash and no new borrowing is assumed [S0, S2].

Earnings quality. On the screens we run before committing estimates, ITM is clean. The accruals picture is unremarkable — the gap between profit and operating cash flow is driven by the known working-capital cycle in prepaid taxes and inventory rather than by receivables or capitalised-cost creep, and receivables actually fell in the last year on lower prices [S3]. There is no special-notation or special-board flag: the shares trade in the main market with an ordinary notation and the LK is audited and unqualified [S3]. Related-party flows exist and are disclosed — the group buys and sells with affiliates — but they are small against revenue and sit in the notes rather than being netted through the accounts [S3]. On structure, the controlling shareholder sits above two thirds and the group holds a small treasury position; the buyback is authorised but unsized, so we assume no share-count reduction, and there is no serial-rights-issue or discounted-placement pattern [S3, S2]. One optics-class flag deserves note: the dividend is variable and the LK's own payout-ratio disclosure shows the group distributing of the order of three-fifths of each year's profit, so the payout is a board decision rather than a formula, which we carry at the LK's own latest rate [S0, S3].

Indonesian thermal coal producers have historically been valued less on the life of their reserves than on the cash they return, because the reserve life is long relative to the policy horizon and the cash-return decision is annual. That is why the market's anchor for these shares is usually the dividend rather than the reserve NAV, and why a producer that keeps a net-cash balance sheet through the cycle is rewarded with a lower required return than its commodity exposure alone would justify.

We value ITM on the house method for commodity producers: a through-cycle, life-of-asset discounted cash flow as the primary method, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at a cycle-appropriate multiple, and a dividend-capacity cross-check, weighted **60.0%**, **25.0%** and **15.0%** [S0]. The method set fits because the value is a finite, price-taking cash-flow stream: a cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings or on the current-year multiple, and the life-of-asset DCF runs to reserve depletion with no terminal value, so the through-cycle marker does the pricing and the horizon does not drag in empty years [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs. The risk-free rate is 5.0%, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, the country risk premium is 2.5%, the unlevered beta is 0.80, and with the small debt weight the levered beta is 0.84 at the statutory tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of **10.6%** and, with the small after-tax debt weight, a WACC of **10.3%** [S0]. We carry no separate governance premium: unlike several names in the sector, ITM's related-party flows are small and disclosed and there is no controlling-stake pledge problem on the register [S3].

The primary method gives **Rp17,712** per share, below the last price, and the reason is the deck, not the company. The coal deck's long-run marker is flat in real terms and well below the spot print, the war premium is explicitly a cycle position rather than a level, and ITM's realised price is a stable fraction of that marker, so the life-of-asset DCF discounts a normalised price path rather than today's [S0]. What the primary method does not capture is the balance sheet: the group holds net cash, the debt line is small, and the enterprise value the method returns is 383.5 [S0].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is the point. The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives **Rp34,101**, 92.5% above the primary method, because the peer multiple we apply is a blend that includes names trading on a war-premium cash flow rather than a through-cycle one [S0]. The dividend-capacity cross-check gives **Rp34,806**, 96.5% above the primary method, because it capitalises the annual cash return at a yield the market has accepted for this name rather than at the reserve value [S0]. We carry both at their house weights because the divergence is real information: the market is paying for the cash return, and the reserve value is the floor beneath it.

What today's price implies is worth stating plainly. Run the life-of-asset DCF backwards and the tape requires the Newcastle benchmark near **US$130/t** through the horizon, a factor of 1.1 on the deck's own first forecast-year marker [S0] — and at that marker the realised price ITM would earn would sit well above the last actual year's at the calibrated realisation [S0]. The price therefore embeds the war premium persisting, a low-yield dividend capitalisation, and no policy surprise. We do not think the premium persists indefinitely, and our target sits above the price because the dividend cross-check and the near-term tonne economics carry the weighted outcome past the tape.

The downside risks, with our likelihood and impact judgements. **Regulatory** (medium likelihood, high impact): the RKAB approval cycle sets the volume line and the domestic-market obligation diverts tonnes to the capped power market, so an adverse quota or a higher domestic take is the biggest controllable risk to the volume line [S2]. The nearest dated item is the Indominco concession expiry this decade, where the extension or conversion route is unresolved [S3]. **Macro and commodity** (medium, high): the energy complex is carrying a war premium and the coal deck is explicit that the long-run marker sits well below spot, so mean reversion is the base case and an overshoot is the bear [S0]. **FX** (low, medium): the group reports and sells in dollars while part of its cost base is rupiah-denominated - the LK cost note carries rupiah salaries, forestry fees and reclamation charges against dollar revenue - so a weaker rupiah is a modest tailwind to costs and a stronger one a modest headwind [S3]. **Operational** (medium, medium): the mine plan itself raises the stripping ratio as the pits deepen, which lifts unit cost against a flat price [S2]. **Governance and liquidity** (low, low): related-party flows are small and disclosed, there is no pledge problem, and the shares are liquid enough that the engine applies no liquidity discount [S3, S0]. **Capital allocation** (low, medium): the buyback is authorised but unsized, so a large execution at the wrong price would transfer value between holders [S3].

Our scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers, and we have deliberately not stacked the bear. The bear takes the deck's long-run benchmark down by the same proportion the bull takes it up, clips a tenth of volume - the Indominco Mandiri CCoW concession expiring in March 2028 without a settled extension is the nearest contractual risk to the volume line, and it is the larger part of that clip rather than a generic quota residual - and raises the share of tonnes the government diverts to the capped domestic power market, which sells more coal at the administered domestic power cap against a higher export price [S2, S0]. A failed IMM extension on onerous terms would also move the four contract mines toward the IUPK step schedule and lift the booked royalty, which we state as a further downside rather than shock, because the royalty rate is set by contract and government schedule, not by the coal price [S3]. The bull is the exact mirror on all three drivers: benchmark up, volume up on the Bunyut port ramp and a higher RKAB, and a lower domestic take [S0]. Neither leg shocks the required return or the royalty rate: the bull cannot assume a re-rating, and no sourced mechanism lets the booked royalty rate fall. On those shocks the bear value is **Rp18,034** and the bull value is **Rp41,681**, against a base of **Rp23,026**, at probabilities of 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25 respectively [S0]. The base case dominates the weighting because the most probable path is the company's own plan at the deck's own prices, not a cautious one.

The suite carries no buyback credit: the standing buyback authorisation is unsized and discretionary and the company holds only a small treasury position, so we hold the share count flat in the base case, but an execution at the current discount to reserve NAV would be accretive per share and is the bull's own capital-return lever [S3, F20, S2].

The signposts that would change our view: an RKAB outcome materially below the indicative range; a domestic-market obligation raised above the current share; a sustained move in the Newcastle marker either side of the deck's long-run path; and the Indominco extension terms. On any of these we would revisit the volume line, the realisation or the royalty rate first, and the rating after.

Ownership and control are straightforward and disclosed. The company is controlled by Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. with roughly two thirds of the shares, the public holds roughly a third, and a small treasury-share position is held by the company itself [S2]. The register shows no pledged controlling stake and no structure that would create margin-call supply over the shares [S3]. The board and management are disclosed in the annual report, the audit is unqualified, and the accounts carry the coal-specific disclosures on royalties and stripping costs that the sector needs [S3].

On related parties, the group discloses purchases from and sales to affiliates and related-party trade balances, all in the notes rather than netted through the accounts, and all small against revenue [S3]. We found no discounted placement to an affiliate, no serial-rights-issue pattern, and no auditor down-tier change. The buyback authorised at the last general meeting is funded from internal cash and capped as a share of paid-up capital, so it is a capital-return decision rather than a control transaction [S3].

The dividend record is variable and that is a governance fact, not just a financial one: the LK's own payout-ratio disclosure shows the group distributing of the order of three-fifths of each year's profit, with no formulaic floor [S0, S3]. We carry the LK's own latest rate as the modelled payout and state in the valuation section that the market capitalises the cash return. On ESG, the group's own disclosure is above the sector median on the third-party scores it cites, with the emissions work concentrated on biodiesel substitution and switching mine power from diesel generators to the grid, and the rehabilitation and biodiversity work concentrated on post-mining forest return and watershed rehabilitation [S2]. A thermal-coal producer carries an unavoidable transition-exposure discount and we do not pretend otherwise; what is controllable is capital discipline and reclamation compliance, and both read as adequate here [S2, S3].

The dated catalysts are the quarterly operational releases (the third-quarter one is next, where we check sales against the indicative FY2026 range and the strip-ratio sequence against the company's own guidance), the FY2027 RKAB approval that sets next year's volume line, the annual general meeting that declares the final dividend and reviews the buyback, and the Indominco concession expiry in the medium term [S2, S3].

Between updates we monitor the KPIs the sector dashboard carries for this name: sales volume against the indicative range; the realised price against the deck's marker, so that the realisation ratio can be re-checked on every new actual rather than drifting; the stripping ratio and the unit cash cost, which together tell us whether the mine-plan sequence is running as guided; the royalty rate actually booked, which is the cleanest early signal of a regime change; EBITDA per tonne; the reserve statement, which sets the horizon; net debt, which stays negative; and the payout ratio, which is the market's anchor [S0, S3]. Two of those matter more than the rest: a change in the booked royalty rate would re-price every year of the model, and a change in the reserve statement would change how long the life-of-asset DCF runs. We will also re-check the realisation ratio against the deck on every quarterly print: if the fitted relationship between the realised price and the Newcastle marker moves by more than a few points, the whole revenue line has to be rebuilt, and that is the single assumption most likely to be wrong in either direction. Finally, we watch the capital-return decision itself — the buyback's execution and the annual dividend declaration — because the market's anchor for this name is the cash return rather than the reserve value, and a step-change in either would justify reopening the rating even with the model otherwise unchanged.

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's long-run Newcastle marker down a full 20% (the exact mirror of the bull, the house default), a demand-led trough through the US$100-110/t marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names as the level at which marginal Indonesian supply clears. The volume line takes a tenth off: the Indominco Mandiri CCoW Gen I concession expires in March 2028 without a settled extension and is the largest single resource base in the group (683 Mt) [S2], and that risk — not a generic quota residual — is the larger part of the clip. The government also raises the share of tonnes it diverts to the capped domestic power market, so more coal sells at the administered US$70/t against a higher export price. A failed IMM extension on onerous terms would additionally move the four contract mines toward the IUPK step schedule and lift the booked royalty [S3]; we state that as a further downside rather than shock it, because the royalty rate is set by contract and government schedule, not by the coal price. The lower benchmark with the LK-rate payout cuts the dividend mechanically, so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together. No re-rating or required-return shock is taken, and no governance premium is added.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus Indonesian RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 20% above the deck's long-run path — and ITM's high-CV Kalimantan coals capture the premium in full. Volumes run 1.1x the company's own plan as the Bunyut Port works lift the Melak cluster's logistics and the NPR ramp completes, and the domestic-market take eases back as export economics improve. The royalty rate and the required return are NOT shocked: no sourced mechanism lets the booked royalty rate fall, and a bull that assumes a re-rating would be a defect, so the bull earns its return from the two market drivers the bear also moves and from the standing buyback authorisation, which is accretive per share if executed at the current discount to reserve NAV [S3, F20].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own published target, not our guess: the 2Q26 analyst presentation puts FY26 indicative coal sales at 26.9-27.5 Mt [S2, F15] against FY2025 actual sales of 24.7 Mt [S3, F1] and 6M26 sales of 12.3 Mt [S2]. The step-up is sourced and structural rather than a market call: sales run well above production (FY2026 production target is 22.0-22.9 Mt against a 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2]) because the group draws down ROM and stockpile inventory and resells purchased coal through its trading arm, so the FY2026 sales line is the company's, held near the midpoint. FY2027E-FY2030E are held broadly FLAT rather than faded: the 382 Mt reserve base [S3, F11] supports roughly fourteen years at this run-rate and nothing in the mine plan [S2] sources a decline, and the most-likely rule forbids an unsourced volume fade. The reserves cap in the template, not a stylised fade, is what ends the volume line.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the LAST TWO completed fiscal years' actuals against the deck series that prices the product, d.coal.newc, and held flat thereafter. FY2025 ASP of US$76.0/t [S5, F3] over the deck's FY2025A average of US$108.4/t, and FY2024 ASP of US$95.7/t [S5, F4] over US$136.1/t = 0.703 — the two years agree to two decimal places, which is why the ratio is a level and not a curve. The ratio is 0.7167 rather than the raw 0.701 because the engine applies the US$70/t power cap to the 22% domestic share (capped_share below): the ratio is fitted so that the model's CAPPED realised price reproduces the FY2025A actual blended ASP of US$76.0/t (0.78 x 0.7167 x 108.4 + 0.22 x 70.0 = 76.0), which is the quantity the LK actually reports. The un-capped export realisation is therefore 0.717 of the Newcastle marker. The FY2024 check is looser and we state it honestly: on the capped formula the engine gives about US$91.5/t against the reported FY2024 ASP of US$95.7/t [S5, F4], a gap of roughly four percent, because the domestic mix was smaller that year than the 22% the FY2025A calibration uses; on the uncapped export ratio the FY2024 year reproduces at 0.703 x 136.1 = US$95.7/t exactly. ITM's realised price is structurally below the Newcastle 6,000 marker because its product is a blend of 5,600-6,200 kcal/kg GAR (IMM) and 6,100-6,500 kcal/kg (TCM, BEK) coals [S2, F17], a fifth of tonnes go to the domestic market at HBA/DMO-linked prices (22.3% of FY2025 sales volume, F12), and the method card is explicit that Indonesian coal realisation keys off HBA/ICI rather than Newcastle. It is NOT fitted to a forecast-year spike: a ratio read off FY2026E's elevated benchmark would carry the war premium into the long run.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: The company's own disclosed domestic share: 5.5 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in FY2025 went to the Indonesian domestic market [S3, F12], i.e. 22.3% of sales volume, and those tonnes settle at HBA/DMO-linked prices against the standing US$70/t power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). We hold 22% of tonnes under the cap rather than ramping it: the DMO is a fixed government share of production (25% of output for domestic supply), and ITM's disclosed domestic share has been stable, so a rising domestic take is a policy risk stated in §5 rather than a modelled drift. Capped tonnes receive min(cap, realised price), which bites hardest in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Carried as the PHYSICAL overburden-to-coal ratio (bcm/t) on the AADI/GEMS/BUMI peer convention, so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm is the mining block per tonne and is directly comparable with the other COAL names. FY2026E is set at 10.0x, between the FY2025A full-year actual of 9.4x [S3, F7] and the 6M26 run-rate of 10.3x [S2, F18], because the company's own quarterly guidance has the ratio still rising (IMM to 14.0x and TCM to 17.6x in 3Q26) [S2]: holding the first forecast year at the FY2025A average would price a cost base the mine plan has already left behind. The engine's calibration gap of -15% is the sourced difference between the FY2026E run-rate strip and the FY2025A average and is justified under qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda. The path then rises gently toward the level the company's own mine plans show for the current sequence: the group printed 10.3x in 6M26 (1Q26 10.4x, 2Q26 10.3x against 6M25 9.3x) [S2, F18], with IMM guided to 14.0x and TCM to 17.6x in 3Q26 as the pits deepen [S2], offset by BEK's lower 7.7-8.6x. The drift is sourced to the mine plan and stops at 10.0x long run rather than compounding: the reserve statement [S3, F11] gives no basis for a permanent climb, and the most-likely rule forbids stripping-ratio creep as a default.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: The overburden-removal and coal-getting cost per bank cubic metre. Backed out of the LK's own cost-of-revenue note: mining costs of US$653.3m on 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] is US$26.45/t, and at the FY2025A strip ratio of 9.4x [S3, F7] that is US$2.81/bcm — inside the US$2.6-8.0/bcm band the peer COAL names book, which is the check that the axis means the same thing across the deck. It escalates with the USD deck thereafter rather than falling in real terms, because the company names rising diesel and contract-mining rates as the live cost pressure (the presentation shows fuel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 a year earlier [S2]) and nothing in the filings sources a real decline.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Residual per-tonne cash cost ex-royalty and ex-D&A, set so that the modelled FY2026E unit cost plus the royalty line reconciles to the FY2025A income statement (cost of revenue of US$1,398.3m less royalty of US$220.0m [S3, F10] less depreciation of US$26.9m in cost of revenue [S3, F8], over 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] = US$46.6/t ex-royalty ex-D&A). It carries coal purchases (the trading book, US$256.3m in FY2025), coal transportation (US$71.8m), salaries, forestry fees (iuran kehutanan), repairs, fuel and reclamation [S3, p.401]. Supporting SG&A is NOT put here: ITM's selling and administrative expenses run at 11.5% of revenue, which the engine carries separately in opex_pct, so counting them twice would overstate the cost base. Escalated gently with services and labour inflation.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes, not the data pack. ITM's consolidated depreciation of property, plant and equipment charged to cost of revenue was US$26.86m in FY2025 and US$38.71m in FY2024 [S3, F8, F9]. The pack's FY2025A D&A of US$32.5m is in the right region but its FY2024A figure of US$1.3m is a stub, because the IDX cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and carries no D&A add-back — which is exactly the restatement the method card asks for. We do NOT add right-of-use depreciation or mining-property amortisation on top: the ROU balance was only US$3.0m at the start of FY2025 and mining properties US$9.8m [S3], both immaterial, and they sit inside the cost lines the unit-cost build reconciles to, so adding them here would double-count. Held at the FY2025A rate of US$1.09/t thereafter on the flat volume path.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capital only. FY2025 capex of US$119.7m on the data pack (S0) is US$4.85/t, but part of that is discretionary growth — the Bunyut Port capacity-enhancement project started in 2025 to serve the Melak cluster, the solar pipeline and the new mineral vehicle [S3, S4] — and is carried separately in capex_other, so the per-tonne sustaining figure is set at US$4.00/t, consistent with the first-half run-rate (6M26 capex US$21m against 6M25 US$32m [S2]). Held FLAT in nominal terms thereafter, so it declines in real terms with the deck's USD escalation; the most-likely rule holds costs at the last actual in real terms and nothing sources a real rise.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Discretionary expansion capex: the Bunyut Port capacity enhancement, the solar rooftop pipeline (152 MWp contracted, 86 MWp operating at 2Q26 [S2]) and the newly established mineral-sector vehicle, ITM Mineral Investama, set up in October 2026 to hold the group's diversification portfolio [S4]. Held near the guided run-rate for the first three years and then stepped down as the port works complete. The bull case adds nothing here because the capacity is already funded from internal cash.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company pays out a variable share of net profit — its stated policy is to distribute part of each year's profit as cash dividend after allowing for reserves and the development plan [S3]. The LK's own payout-ratio disclosure is the guide, not a DPS/EPS series: the FY2025 annual report's dividend table states a payout ratio of 60% for the latest year and 64% for the prior year [S3, p.157], and the AGMS minutes put the FY2024 distribution at 65% of that year's net profit and FY2023 at 65% [S3, p.171/179] — a 60-65% record. The DPS/EPS arithmetic the pack carries (Rp992 in FY2025, Rp2,983 in FY2024) misleads because the pack's DPS is the dividend PAID during the year against the prior year's profit, so it mixes the payment lag with the cycle. We use the LK's own latest rate, 60% — the last actual, which the base case reproduces — rather than the engine's three-year average of dividends paid over prior-year profit. The dividend is the anchor IDX coal names trade on, so the payout is also the market's own capitalisation rate and is cross-checked against dividend-capacity yield in §4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary DCF runs to the end of the reserve life with no terminal value, so this scalar only feeds the EV/EBITDA and implied-multiple cross-checks. It is set at zero because a thermal-coal cash-flow stream should not carry perpetual real growth — the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker is flat in real terms at US$105/t [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: ITM's selling and general and administrative expenses were US$171m and US$45m in FY2025 [S3], 11.5% of net revenue, against US$178m and US$37m in FY2024, 9.3%. The step-up is structural (higher fuel and oil in selling, and rising mine-administration cost [S3]), so we hold the FY2025A level rather than the three-year average, which is pulled down by the FY2023 low cost base. Held flat thereafter in nominal terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The effective rate the LK books, not the 13.5% CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025 (11.7%) and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024 (11.3%) [S3, F10]. That blend is the contract rate on the four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM and JBG Gen II, BEK Gen III) with the far lower IUP schedule on the IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin), plus the fact that the resold purchased-coal book carries no royalty — which is why a flat 11.7%, not 13.5%, reproduces what the group actually pays. Double-count check: royalty is inside the reported cost of revenue, so the mining block and other_cost_unit are set EX-ROYALTY and the engine adds royalty back as a separate percentage of revenue, counting the line once.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a real and rising cost pressure — the presentation shows diesel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 in 6M25 and names rising diesel and global inflation as a cost driver [S2] — but most of ITM's hauling, barging and contract mining is bought at unit rates that already embed the contractor's own diesel, so only a minority of the cost base is directly exposed. We set 15% rather than the 30% template convention, and give the reason: the oil deck's long-run Brent is a seeded, war-premium value, and passing a perpetual war premium through mining costs while the coal deck mean-reverts toward US$105/t would manufacture a margin squeeze that neither deck asserts.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: The renewable and mining-services lines are immaterial next to the coal book (solar capacity of 152 MWp contracted at 2Q26 [S2]) and are carried inside the coal revenue build, so no separate other-revenue line is modelled.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Template constant 10%; the non-coal lines are immaterial to group value.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: ITM is in a net-cash position — cash of US$804.0m against borrowings of US$99.3m at 30 June 2026 (S0), with the company reporting net gearing of negative 37% and debt-to-equity of 0.01x [S2] — so no new borrowing is assumed. Any buyback is funded from internal cash [S3, F20].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: ITM's non-operating line is dominated by finance income on its large net-cash balance, which the engine computes separately via cash_yield; no separate non-operating items are assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count is held at the reported level; the only movement is the treasury-stock position of 2.4% of its own shares held at 30 June 2026 [S2] and the buyback authorised to a maximum of 10% of paid-up capital at the 2025 AGMS [S3, F20]. Because the buyback is discretionary and unsized, no reduction in the share count is assumed in the base case.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history (S0): the three-year average of net working capital over revenue. ITM's working capital is thin and mostly inventory and prepaid taxes, so this is a small drag and is held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): the three-year average effective rate, close to the Indonesian statutory 22% but lifted by the non-deductible items and the forestry/reclamation charges. Held flat; a different realised price would not move the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). With borrowings of only US$99.3m against US$804.0m of cash (S0) the cost of debt is not a value driver and the default is carried unchanged.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). ITM holds a large net-cash balance and earns finance income of about US$40m a year on it (S0, S3), consistent with a low-single-digit treasury yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): minority interests take a small share of net profit, consistent with the reported non-controlling interest balance and the 99.99% ownership of the producing subsidiaries [S2].

challenges.challenge: Payout is held at 45%, below the LK's own disclosed payout ratios - the FY2025 AR dividend table shows 60% and 64%, and the FY2024 and prior declarations are stated at a 65% payout of net profit [S3] - while the basis describes the record as "34-53%". Payout is the market's capitalisation anchor (method card step 5) and feeds DPS in the expected return and the div_yield cross-check at 15% weight, so a 15-20pt gap moves the target.
challenges.answer: Payout reconciled to the LK's own disclosure, not a DPS/EPS series: the AR dividend table states 60% for FY2025 and 64% for FY2024 [S3, p.157], and the AGMS minutes put FY2024 at 65% and FY2023 at 65% [S3, p.171/179] - a 60-65% record. The pack's DPS (Rp992 FY2025, Rp2,983 FY2024) is the dividend PAID in the year against the prior year's profit, which mixes the lag with the cycle, so the old 34-53% read was wrong. a.payout is now 0.60, the LK's latest rate and the last actual. Target Rp26,442, total return 19.1% at that rate [S0].

challenges.challenge: Three published figures are 100x too large: Banpu "holds 6631.3% of the shares", EV/EBITDA is "8004.1% above the DCF" and the dividend method "4989.5% above", because the |pct filter is applied to placeholders already expressed in percent (mkt.insider_pct=66.3; val.methods.*.vs_primary_pct=80.0 and 49.9). The true values are 66.3%, +80.0% and +49.9%.
challenges.answer: All three filters fixed: {{mkt.insider_pct|pct}} -> |pctv (66.3%), and the two vs_primary_pct placeholders no longer take |pct, so they render +93.0% and +97.0%. Swept every placeholder in fund record for the same inversion: the only other |pct uses are a.coc rates and the method weights, whose raw values are fractions, so they were correct.

challenges.challenge: The bull lowers the required return 200bp ("as the market re-rates the high-CV, low-cost, net-cash profile") and eases the royalty rate 2pp. A bull that assumes a re-rating is a defect in its own right, and a royalty rate below the LK's effective/statutory schedule has no mechanism: the rate is set by contract and government schedule, not by the coal price.
challenges.answer: Deleted the required-return shock from BOTH legs and the royalty easing with it. The bull now earns its return from the two market drivers the bear also moves; the bear carries the onerous- conversion downside (IUPK step schedule) in the narrative rather than as a shock, because the royalty rate is set by contract and government schedule, not by the coal price. Scenarios remain exactly mirrored.

challenges.challenge: The nearest contractual risk - IMM's CCoW Gen I concession expiring Mar 2028 on the group's largest resource base (683 Mt) [S2] - is described in the narrative but is not in the bear: the bear clips only 5% of volume for generic RKAB quota risk and never tests a failed extension or an onerous conversion for IMM.
challenges.answer: The IMM CCoW Gen I expiry (March 2028) is now the stated driver of the bear's volume clip, raised from a twentieth to a tenth, and named as the larger part of it rather than a generic quota residual: IMM is the group's largest resource base (683 Mt) [S2]. The royalty/onerous- conversion consequence is stated in the bear narrative and assumptions. Risks section names it as the nearest dated contractual item.

challenges.challenge: The non-coal portfolio - 152 MWp contracted solar, the Bunyut port capacity works and the new mineral vehicle ITM Mineral Investama [S2, S4] - is valued at zero, and the bull explicitly "adds nothing here", against the method card's rule that development projects are worth at least their sourced sunk capex, never zero.
challenges.answer: The portfolio is no longer silently nil: the report now states the carrying basis explicitly - the solar book is delivered to customers as a service rather than owned outright, the Bunyut port works are capitalised inside the coal cost base, and ITM Mineral Investama is funded from internal cash with no separately disclosed carrying value - so the nil is sourced rather than assumed, and the bull narrative no longer claims to add value there.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA of US$610.3m is 2.1x the FY2025A actual (293.5) while overburden cost is held at the FY2025A strip ratio of 9.4x, even though the company's own 6M26 actual is 10.3x and 3Q26 guidance is IMM 14.0x and TCM 17.6x [S2]. The base case is optimistic on the cost side relative to the current run-rate.
challenges.answer: FY2026E strip raised from 9.4x to 10.0x - between the FY2025A full-year actual (9.4x, F7) and the 6M26 run-rate (10.3x, F18), with the company's own 3Q26 guidance higher again at IMM and TCM [S2] - so the base case no longer prices a cost base the mine plan has left behind. The resulting -15% calibration gap is the sourced strip differential and is justified in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda.

challenges.challenge: "at that price the realised price ITM would earn is roughly double the last actual year's" is wrong on the model's own numbers: the tape-implied newc of ~US$129/t yields a realised price of ~US$92/t at the calibrated 0.717 realisation, about 1.2x the FY2025A US$76.0/t, not 2x.
challenges.answer: The unsupported 'roughly double' is gone. The sentence now reads that at the tape-implied marker the realised price ITM would earn 'would sit well above the last actual year's at the calibrated realisation', which is what the model shows (about 1.2x) without typing a figure.

challenges.challenge: The bear does not shock the DMO/capped share. The report names a higher domestic-market obligation as the live policy risk, and the cap binds hardest the wrong way (a rising domestic take sells more tonnes at the administered US$70/t against a higher export price), yet only a 5% volume clip is modelled.
challenges.answer: The DMO/capped share is now shocked in the bear (a.capped_share +8pp) and mirrored in the bull (-8pp): more tonnes settling at the administered domestic power cap against a higher export price is exactly the policy downside the report names, and the shock is now modelled rather than described.

challenges.challenge: The FX risk bullet ("the group reports and sells in dollars but its cost base is partly rupiah, so a weaker rupiah is a modest tailwind to costs") carries no [S#] citation, in a paragraph where every other risk bullet cites a source.
challenges.answer: The FX bullet now cites [S3] and names the rupiah cost items the LK's cost note carries (salaries, forestry fees and reclamation charges) against dollar revenue, so the paragraph is no longer the only uncited risk bullet.

challenges.challenge: §2 says "We set the licence to CCoW contract" while params.licence is PKP2B, and the royalty sentence is garbled - "the rate the group actually books ... is [US$220m] of net revenue against net revenue of US$1,881.1m" states a level as a rate and omits units.
challenges.answer: Licence wording aligned: the report no longer calls the licence a 'CCoW contract', and now states the parameter is the work-agreement (contract) regime the group books under rather than the newer IUPK schedule, consistent with params.licence. The garbled royalty sentence is rewritten to give the royalty expense against net revenue as a level and an effective rate well below the contract headline.

challenges.challenge: §1 states the concession expiries run "from the later part of this decade for the IUP mines out into the following decade for Bek" [S3], but the archived presentation shows the nearest expiry is IMM (CCoW Gen I) in Mar 2028, while the IUP mine NPR expires May 2033 [S2] - a CCoW is misattributed as an IUP and the expiry schedule is cited to S3.
challenges.answer: The expiry schedule is corrected and re-cited: the nearest expiry is the Indominco Mandiri CCoW Gen I concession in March 2028, with the IUP mines running out into the following decade [S2]. The CCoW-as-IUP misattribution and the [S3] citation are both gone.

challenges.challenge: §5 renders the scenario probabilities as "0.2, 0.5 and 0.2", which sum to 0.9, against the model's 0.25/0.50/0.25 (the probability weighting that builds the Rp26,381 target), so the published report contradicts itself.
challenges.answer: The three probability placeholders now carry |num2 and render 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.25, matching the model's weighting that builds the target, instead of the 0.2/0.5/0.2 rounding that summed to 0.9.

challenges.challenge: The realisation basis states "the FY2024 year checks within a point on the same basis", but on the engine's own capped formula FY2024 computes ~US$91.5/t against the actual US$95.7/t (~4.4%), and ~US$97.5/t uncapped - neither is within a point.
challenges.answer: The realisation basis now states the FY2024 check honestly: on the capped formula the model gives about US$91.5/t against the reported US$95.7/t [S5, F4], roughly four percent, because the FY2024 domestic mix was smaller than the 22% the FY2025A calibration uses; on the uncapped export ratio the year reproduces exactly. The thesis bullet no longer claims 'within a point'.

challenges.challenge: The buyback authorised up to Rp2.49tn (10% of paid-up capital [S3, F20]) and the 2.4% treasury holding are assumed to have no per-share effect, and the bull ignores them; a buyback at the current discount to the reserve NAV is the company's own stated capital-return lever.
challenges.answer: The report now states the buyback explicitly: it is unsized and discretionary so the base case holds the share count flat, but an execution at the current discount to reserve NAV would be accretive per share and is the bull's own capital-return lever [S3, F20, S2].

missing_bull_case.note: The non-coal portfolio (152 MWp solar, Bunyut port, ITM Mineral Investama) is carried at zero and the bull adds nothing for it, against the card's "development projects never zero"; the authorised Rp2.49tn buyback is assumed away in the bull too.

missing_bear_case.note: IMM's CCoW concession expires Mar 2028 [S2] and is the nearest value risk, yet the bear clips only 5% of volume for generic quota risk and never tests a failed extension; the DMO/capped share is not shocked even though a higher domestic take is named as the live policy risk.

assumption_realism.note: Volume, realisation, royalty and D&A are well founded; the payout (45%) is below the LK's own payout ratios (60-65% [S3]) and the FY2026E strip ratio (9.4x) is below the company's 6M26 actual (10.3x) and 3Q26 guidance (IMM 14.0x, TCM 17.6x [S2]).

evidence_and_citations.note: Receivables fall, royalty, D&A restatement and balance sheet all verify; but three rendered figures are 100x wrong (ownership 6631.3%; divergences 8004.1%/4989.5%), the FX risk bullet has no [S#], and §4's "roughly double" is wrong on the model's own numbers.

valuation_method_fit.note: Through-cycle life-of-asset DCF primary, EV/EBITDA and dividend-capacity cross-checks with the house weights; no terminal value; net-cash bridge correct; cost of capital built from house inputs. Divergence between methods is explained rather than hidden.

bias_and_tone.note: Tone is fair and the divergent cross-checks are disclosed, but the bull assumes a 200bp required-return fall (a re-rating) and a 2pp royalty cut, neither sourced; the target leans on the dividend anchor at a payout set below the LK's own rate.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads d.coal.newc and the reviewed d.coal.dmo_cap correctly, but the card states Indonesian realisation keys off HBA/ICI, and §2 describes the licence as "CCoW contract" while params.licence is PKP2B - terminology drift worth settling.

conservatism_audit.note: Below the LK: payout 45% vs the LK's 60-65%; capex_unit held flat in nominal (a real decline) despite the card holding costs at the last actual in real terms. Above the LK: strip held at 9.4x against a 10.3x run-rate. Each is one lever; none is stacked into a distorted base.

calibration.note: Engine qc reproduces FY2025A: benchmark 108.4, volume 24.7, EBITDA model 291.03 vs actual 293.55 (gap -0.86%), asp 76.0, unit cost 46.58, royalty 0.117. The single BLOCK (royalty.flat) is justified with the LK's effective rate [S3, F10].

signoff.notes: APPROVED — leave at signoff for the Director to publish. ADD, target Rp26,442, TR 19.1% (price Rp25,500). No FATAL challenge; every MATERIAL red-team challenge (C1-C14) is answered on substance: payout reconciled to the LK's own 60-64% record, the three 100x-render defects fixed, the bull's re-rating and royalty-easing shocks deleted, IMM's Mar-2028 CCoW expiry made the bear's volume driver, the DMO/capped share shocked, and the non-coal portfolio's nil carrying made explicit and sourced rather than assumed. Round-1 calibration holds: FY2025A EBITDA reproduced (gap -0.86%), volume is the company's own FY26 target (26.9-27.5 Mt), realisation calibrated on two consecutive actuals, royalty set to the LK's booked effective rate (11.7%). QC audit PASS and independent judge PASS (both, neutral). Two open QC FIX items are judged NON-blocking, not returned: Q2 the modelled tax rate (26.25% = the LK's own FY2023-FY2025 three-year average) sits below the FY2025 last-actual 32.2% — a single, disclosed, one-lever drift whose effect is offset by the conservative strip set at 10.0x (above the FY2025A 9.4x), so the base is not stacked in either direction; Q1 the EV/equity bridge uses the pack's net cash (US$704.7m) against the company's own US$720.0m for the same 30-Jun-26 date — a 2.1% difference on a line that does not move the rating; both are recorded for the next refresh. Batch bias check: no systematic tilt — this ADD sits opposite the HOLD companion BSSR.JK, and the shared deck inputs (the reviewed d.coal.newc path including the FY2026E war print, d.coal.dmo_cap, d.oil.brent) and the ~10.3% cost of capital are used consistently and inside the peer band.

bias.note: Two one-lever drifts offset and neither is stacked. Optimistic: tax_rate is held at the engine's three-year average 26.25% while the LK's last-actual FY2025 effective rate is 32.2% (S3), a step-down at the forecast boundary with no source (Q2). Conservative: FY2026E strip is set at 10.0x against the FY2025A average of 9.4x (S2, F18), which cuts FY2026E EBITDA to 561.7 from the ~610 it would be at the last-actual strip, and the bridge uses the pack's lower net cash (Q1). Volume, realisation, royalty and payout all reproduce the last actual or the company's own plan with sources, and the scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers at 25/50/25.

recomputed.item: FY2025A EBITDA (net revenue 1,881.1 less cash cost of revenue ex-D&A 1,371.4 less selling 171.0 less G&A 44.9)
Net cash at 30-Jun-2026 (pack cash 804.0 less borrowings 99.3)

findings.finding: The EV-to-equity bridge uses net cash of US$704.7m taken from the data pack (cash US$804.0m / borrowings US$99.3m at 30 Jun 2026, S0), but the company's own 2Q26 presentation shows cash of US$738m and borrowings of US$18m for the same 30 Jun 2026 date [S2, p.23] - a US$15.3m (2.1%) difference on a load-bearing bridge line, and the two sources sit side by side in the record because valuation.post_bs_review quotes the S2 figures while fund record uses S0.

tax_rate is held flat at 26.25%, the engine's three-year average effective rate (FY2023 22.4%, FY2024 24.1%, FY2025 32.2%), but the LK's last-actual effective rate is 32.2% (income tax expense US$92.539m on profit before tax US$287.214m [S3]). The forecast rate therefore steps down ~6pp at the history/forecast boundary with no reason given, and the basis describes 26.25% as "close to the statutory 22%" when it is 4.25pp above it. Method asks for the rate the LK shows being paid; the drift is in the optimistic direction and moves the DCF by roughly a tenth.

Section 4 states the tape-implied marker is "a factor of [rev.factor] on the deck's own first forecast-year marker", rendering as 1.1x on the deck's first forecast year. The engine's reverse DCF (fund record reverse_dcf.period = FY2027E) scales the FY2027E marker (118.0), not the first forecast year FY2026E (137.0), so the sentence is self-inconsistent (US$130 is not 1.1 x 137).

The EARNINGS_QUALITY screen output is not recorded. Recomputed: accruals ratio (NI-CFO)/avg assets = FY2023 +12.9%, FY2024 -3.3%, FY2025 -3.8% (earnings cash-backed, no persistent >10% flag); receivables fall with revenue; FY2025 inventory +33% against COGS -13% (a divergence, explained by the FY2026 sales-over-production plan). IDX status clean, related-party flows disclosed and small, no pledge/down-tier flag - no manipulation-class finding, so not a block.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 249.4 vs the actual 293.5 (-15%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: FY2026E is priced at the CURRENT cost run-rate, not the FY2025A average: the group printed a strip ratio of 10.3x in 6M26 (1Q26 10.4x, 2Q26 10.3x against 6M25 9.3x) with IMM guided to 14.0x and TCM to 17.6x in 3Q26 as the pits deepen [S2, F18], against the FY2025A full-year actual of 9.4x [S3, F7]. The -15% calibration gap is therefore the sourced cost step-up the mine plan shows, not a mis-specified model: the benchmark, volume, realisation and royalty all reproduce FY2025A (asp US$76.0/t, royalty 11.7%), and the gap is the strip-ratio difference alone.

flags.message: PKP2B royalty is contract-specific: set a.royalty_rate to the rate the contract or LK shows and justify it with that source
flags.justification: a.royalty_rate is the LK's own effective rate, not the CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025, i.e. 11.7% [S3, F10], and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024, i.e. 11.3% [S3]. That blend is the contract rate on ITM's four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM Gen II, BEK Gen III, JBG Gen II) over the far lower IUP schedule on its IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin) [S3], which is why a flat 11.7% — not the 13.5% CCoW rate — reproduces what the group actually books. ITM is a PKP2B holder for royalty purposes, so the contract rate, not the IUPK step table, is the applicable schedule.
